title: Calories Burned Calculator: how it works, formula and examples

content:
The [Calories Burned Calculator](/calories-burned-calculator) is a free online tool on CalcHub. Estimate gross exercise calories from body weight, activity duration and standard MET values. Enter your body weight, activity duration and activity and the result appears straight away — no account or download needed. Because it runs entirely in your browser, the values you type never leave your device, and you can use it as often as you like.

A metabolic equivalent of task (MET) expresses activity intensity relative to quiet rest. This calculator uses published representative MET values to estimate energy expenditure for a selected activity, weight and duration. It reports both gross calories and an active-calorie estimate that subtracts approximate resting expenditure, helping explain why fitness apps and gym equipment can show different totals for the same workout. This guide explains how to use it, the formula it applies, and a worked example you can follow with your own numbers.

## How to use the Calories Burned Calculator

Start by entering your body weight (kg), then entering your activity duration (minutes) and finally choosing your activity from the list. The result updates as you type, so adjust any value and watch the answer change. If the answer is not what you expected, check the value you entered first — a missing digit or a wrong unit is the usual cause.

1. Enter current body weight in kilograms and the time spent actively exercising.
2. Choose the closest listed activity and intensity rather than selecting only by activity name.
3. Use gross calories for total energy expenditure or active calories when comparing with a device that excludes resting metabolism.

## Formula

Gross kcal = MET × body weight (kg) × duration (hours). Active kcal ≈ (MET − 1) × kg × hours.

That is the standard formula for this calculation, and it is the same one the [Calories Burned Calculator](/calories-burned-calculator) applies to the values you enter. You can work it out by hand, but the calculator is faster when you want to try several values, and it removes the risk of a slip in the arithmetic.

## Worked example

Here is a typical example. A 75 kg person walking briskly at 3.5 METs for 45 minutes burns about 197 kcal gross. Subtracting estimated resting expenditure gives about 141 active kcal. Try the same figures in the [Calories Burned Calculator](/calories-burned-calculator) and you will get the same result — then change one value at a time to see how the answer moves.

## What the result shows

With the default values (Body weight: 75 kg, Activity duration: 45 minutes, Activity: Brisk walking — 3.5 METs), the [Calories Burned Calculator](/calories-burned-calculator) returns Gross calories burned: 197 kcal, Estimated active calories above rest: 141 kcal, Calories per minute: 4.4 kcal, Selected intensity: 3.5 METs. The first figure is the headline result, and the rest break it down so you can see how the total is made up. If you want to compare with a related calculation, the [BMI Calculator](/bmi-calculator) is worth a look before you finish.

## What one MET means

One MET is conventionally treated as one kilocalorie per kilogram per hour and approximates resting energy use. An activity at 7 METs therefore uses roughly seven times the resting rate. The selected presets are representative values, not measurements of your precise pace, gradient, technique or environment.

## Why estimates differ from wearable devices

Real expenditure changes with fitness, movement efficiency, temperature, stops, terrain and body composition. Wearables add heart-rate or motion models and may estimate active rather than gross energy. Treat the result as a planning estimate and avoid using it as an exact licence to replace every calorie through food.

## Tips

A few things worth knowing before you rely on the result — most of them are about the numbers you put in, rather than the tool itself:

- Use total moving time rather than the length of the whole session if you took long breaks.
- Higher intensity does not always mean more total calories if the duration becomes much shorter.
- For weight management, track trends over weeks rather than reacting to one exercise estimate.

## Frequently asked questions

### How accurate is a MET calorie estimate?

It is useful for general comparisons but can differ materially from measured expenditure. It does not capture individual fitness, exact pace, stops or terrain. For figures that matter, such as money, health or legal deadlines, check the result against an authoritative source before acting on it.

### What is the difference between active and total calories?

Total or gross calories include the energy you would have used at rest during that time. Active calories subtract that resting baseline. Try it with your own numbers in the [Calories Burned Calculator](/calories-burned-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### Should I eat back all exercise calories?

Not automatically. Estimates can be high and appetite varies. If you track energy balance, use consistent methods and judge progress from longer-term trends. Try it with your own numbers in the [Calories Burned Calculator](/calories-burned-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### What formula does the Calories Burned Calculator use?

Gross kcal = MET × body weight (kg) × duration (hours). Active kcal ≈ (MET − 1) × kg × hours. You can see it in action in the [Calories Burned Calculator](/calories-burned-calculator) — enter your own values and the result updates as you type.
